mcqs.question: Why does moving a fast pointer twice as fast as a slow one guarantee they meet if and only if the list has a cycle?
options: If there's no cycle, the fast pointer simply reaches the end first with nothing gained; if there is one, it eventually laps the slow pointer inside the loop and lands on the same node
The two pointers always meet regardless of whether a cycle exists
The fast pointer meets the slow pointer only if the list has an even number of nodes
This only works on doubly linked lists
mcqs.explanation: Without a cycle the fast pointer just terminates first — no meeting occurs. With a cycle, once both pointers are inside the loop the fast one closes the gap by one node per step and can't jump over the slow one, so a meeting is guaranteed within one loop length. It works identically on singly linked lists and doesn't depend on total node count parity.

mcqs.question: After slow and fast meet inside a cycle, why does resetting one pointer to head and advancing both one step at a time land them at the cycle's start?
options: It's a coincidence that happens to work for most test cases
The distance from head to the cycle start equals the distance from the meeting point to the cycle start going forward, a fact derivable from the tortoise/hare distance equations
Because the meeting point is always the cycle's start already
Because resetting a pointer always finds the head of any list
mcqs.explanation: Working out the distances each pointer traveled when they meet shows the head-to-start distance and meeting-point-to-start distance are equal, which is exactly why moving both at the same speed from those two points converges at the start — it's a proven equality, not a heuristic. The meeting point is generally somewhere inside the loop, not at its start.

mcqs.question: Using `while fast and fast.next: slow = slow.next; fast = fast.next.next`, what does `slow` point to once the loop ends for a list with an even number of nodes?
options: The first of the two middle nodes
The second of the two middle nodes
The last node in the list
The node just before the true middle
mcqs.explanation: Because fast covers exactly twice the ground slow does, and the loop only stops once fast can't safely take another double-step, slow ends up on the second of the two middle nodes for even-length lists. Landing on the first middle node instead requires tightening the loop condition to check one node further ahead.

mcqs.question: The O(1)-space palindrome check reverses the second half of the list in place. What must a correct implementation do that's easy to forget?
options: Nothing extra — the answer is correct as soon as the comparison finishes
Convert the list to an array before comparing
Restore the second half to its original order afterward if the caller expects the list unchanged
Reverse the first half instead of the second
mcqs.explanation: The technique intentionally mutates the list to avoid extra space, which gives a correct palindrome answer but leaves the list structurally altered — a caller expecting the original list back needs an explicit re-reversal step, which is easy to skip since the boolean answer already looks right. Converting to an array defeats the O(1)-space goal, and reversing the wrong half breaks the comparison itself.

mcqs.question: Why does `while fast.next and fast:` crash on some odd-length lists while `while fast and fast.next:` does not?
options: There's no difference between the two orderings
Because `and` evaluates right to left in most languages
Because the loop only runs on odd-length lists in the first place
Left-to-right short-circuiting means `fast.next` is evaluated before confirming `fast` isn't None, and `fast` can become None on the very iteration this matters
mcqs.explanation: Most languages evaluate `and` left to right, so the buggy order tries to read `.next` off a possibly-None `fast` before checking it exists — a crash that specifically surfaces when a fast pointer lands on `None` at just the right step, which happens more readily with odd-length lists. The two orderings are not equivalent, and the bug isn't restricted to only running on odd-length lists.

mcqs.question: An interviewer explicitly says "detect the cycle without using extra space." What are they ruling out, and what should you reach for?
options: They're ruling out recursion; use an iterative loop with a visited-node hash set
They're ruling out the hash-set-of-visited-nodes approach, which is O(n) space; reach for fast/slow pointers instead
They're ruling out fast/slow pointers, since those also use extra space
There's no difference between the two approaches on space
mcqs.explanation: A hash set tracking visited node references is the natural first idea for cycle detection but costs O(n) space; explicitly banning extra space signals the interviewer wants the O(1)-space fast/slow pointer technique instead. Fast/slow pointers use only a constant number of references, not O(n) space, so they satisfy the constraint the hash-set approach violates.
